  • Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:.

In a recent development, we evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Recent findings suggest that edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:.

Recent findings suggest that the port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:.

Industry News: The Only Edge Was Memorized in Training: LLM Trading Agents Around Earnings and Bad News

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (275 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.22177v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) trading agents are tested on news, but news reaches stock prices within minutes, and a benchmark that replays headlines at their publication time finds no alpha in trading on them. Money can then remain in two places, before news whose date is known, such as earnings announcements, and after bad news, if the market's fall went too far. However, studies of LLMs and earnings read documents published with or after the announcement, and studies of reversal sort monthly portfolios, so neither tells whether an agent can trade these moments after costs. In this paper, we test LLM agents at both moments on the same look-ahead-free benchmark, before 598 earnings announcements and after 409 bad-news drops of large US stocks. Every input is cut at the decision close, staged agents are compared with single calls, simple rules and a logistic regression, and every decision is made with and without the stock's name. Across five models from four vendors, no agent beat the simple bets. Before earnings, the agents mostly bought and earned what buying before every announcement earned, and after bad news, a Gemini-based agent called almost every fall an overreaction while no agent picked better dips than buying them all. The only gains came from what the models had memorized in training. Given only the ticker and the dates, a GPT-based model called the direction of 59.2% of the announcements before its training cutoff and 53.3% after it. Agent builders should therefore compare an event agent with the simple bet and test it blind after the training cutoff.

On-demand connectivity in minutes, not weeks. Set up your connection from the Google Cloud console or API, pick the bandwidth you need, and both clouds handle the rest — no hardware to order, no manual network configuration, and no back and forth between providers.

Built-in reliability. Your connection runs across physically separate locations for redundancy. Google Cloud and Azure jointly monitor the connection and handle maintenance and recovery for you.

Private and secure. Your traffic stays off the public internet, and is automatically encrypted between the Google Cloud and Azure edge routers, with no customer configuration required.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that AWS IAM Identity Center now gives you the option to require workforce consumers to re-authenticate with your external identity provider (IdP) each time their user interactive session expires.
  • When you set user re-authentication to Required and a user's user interactive session expires, IAM Identity Center prompts the user to re-authenticate with your external IdP.
  • According to recent reports, you can configure user re-authentication for any IAM Identity Center instance (organization or account) that's connected to an external IdP as its identity source.

It has been revealed that AWS IAM Identity Center now gives you the option to require workforce consumers to re-authenticate with your external identity provider (IdP) each time their user interactive session expires. By default, when a user's session expires, IAM Identity Center renews it through the user's existing IdP session, and the user isn't prompted to sign in again. For organizations with strict security or compliance requirements that mandate explicit user verification at regular intervals, this automatic renewal may not meet policy requirements.

When you set user re-authentication to Required and a user's user interactive session expires, IAM Identity Center prompts the user to re-authenticate with your external IdP. This helps you enforce stronger sign-in controls for regulated workloads. IAM Identity Center implements this by adding the SAML 2.0 ForceAuthn attribute to the SAML request sent to your IdP.

According to recent reports, you can configure user re-authentication for any IAM Identity Center instance (organization or account) that's connected to an external IdP as its identity source. The setting applies only to service provider initiated sign-ins, where users sign in through your AWS access portal URL. Changes to the user re-authentication setting are logged in AWS CloudTrail, so you can audit when it was turned on or off.

Recent findings suggest that user re-authentication is available in all AWS Regions where IAM Identity Center is available at no additional cost. To learn more, see Require user re-authentication in the AWS IAM Identity Center User Guide.

arXiv:2611.22174v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: General-purpose behavior models increasingly internalize broad procedural knowledge during training, making their adaptation to new goals and skill interfaces less a problem of learning entirely new behaviors than of reconfiguring existing competence. We study this capability as reconfigurability, the ability to realize new behaviors by cost-efficiently restructuring existing components and relations under sparse governing information, where task specifications provide high-level goals and procedure specifications expose a limited set of reusable factors, leaving the concrete bindings and compositions required for execution underdetermined. We propose RecPo, a framework that represents skills task-agnostically through multiple procedure views and materializes executable skill sequences by composing stored transitions to realize task-specific changes. RecPo maintains a procedure knowledge base of skill-induced transitions, with each view exposing a reusable factor and preserving local skill connectivity. At deployment, it interprets task specifications through the same views and resolves the resulting compositional queries over the stored relations to bind skills for execution. On long-horizon tasks in an extended Franka Kitchen benchmark, RecPo achieves 91.9% ordered completion with 1.0 ms of task inference per episode across varying procedure support and task-record sparsity. Real-robot studies further demonstrate adaptation through local memory edits without task-specific retraining.

The Paris opening builds on the firm’s Luxembourg branch, launched in 2025, and a representative office in Frankfurt that opened in early 2026. Together, these moves form part of the group’s strategy to establish itself as a go-to partner across Europe’s major financial centres.

It has been revealed that prometeia head of risk management area Andrea Partesotti said, “Being selected by Crédit Agricole for a programme of this magnitude is a strong recognition of our growing presence in the market of ALM solutions for Tier1 banking groups. In a recent development, black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):.

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:.

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Recent findings suggest that pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

With several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:.

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

Recent findings suggest that boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

For edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:.

In a recent development, everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:.

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:.

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

It has been revealed that A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:.

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

According to recent reports, A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call.

Recent findings suggest that let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:.

According to recent reports, FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

In a recent development, the text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

Recent findings suggest that this gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:.

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

Sources indicate that at the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Sources indicate that each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

According to recent reports, the noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

According to recent reports, the distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:.

In a recent development, text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:.

The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are latest to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

According to recent reports, get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:.

Readie: Low-Latency Code Sandboxes for AI Agents

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (207 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22171v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: From quantitative research to personal assistance, AI agents act by iteratively generating and executing code. To decouple the agent harness from code execution, many agents offload execution to dedicated systems called code sandboxes. However, existing code sandboxes suffer from slow startup. Whether they rely on custom snapshots or a single fat image, the root cause is the same: it is hard to build a compact, pre-warmed snapshot that can be shared across diverse agent-generated code while covering nearly all the artifacts (e.g., packages, datasets) it requires. In this work, we propose learned startup snapshots for low-latency code sandboxes. Our insight is that while it is hard for a single snapshot to be both compact and cover most workloads, a set of snapshots can achieve both. Each snapshot is small, initializes swiftly, and covers a fraction of agent-generated code; together, the set covers most of it. We learn this set from a large training workload by formulating snapshot construction as an optimization problem and solving it with an approximation algorithm. Planned on 15K public and LLM-synthesized scripts, our system, Readie, reduces startup latency by 3-22$\times$ and end-to-end runtime by 1.3-3.3$\times$ compared to existing approaches at the same storage budget.

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (304 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) now supports Networking Flexible Cost Allocation (FCA), which splits shared networking costs by the resources that actually drive them, so you can see what each team or application used.
  • Today, when several teams share a resource such as a NAT gateway, the account that owns it pays the full cost and can't see which team or application drove it.
  • FCA is available at no additional charge.

Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) now supports Networking Flexible Cost Allocation (FCA), which splits shared networking costs by the resources that actually drive them, so you can see what each team or application used. Until now, AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR), including CUR 2.0 in AWS Data Exports, showed networking usage as a single item, and most customers split it across teams with custom scripts and manual estimates. FCA splits this line item by the resources that generated it. It supports NAT gateway data processing and data transfer, including traffic to the internet, and in-Region Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) and VPC peering data transfer.

Today, when several teams share a resource such as a NAT gateway, the account that owns it pays the full cost and can't see which team or application drove it. To work around this, some customers built custom scripts to analyze VPC Flow Logs, which takes ongoing engineering effort. Others used fixed-percentage splits, which overcharge some teams and undercharge others. FCA breaks down usage based on traffic sources, helping you accurately track financial metrics based on applications and teams. To get started, attach a cost allocation policy to a NAT gateway, VPC peering connection, or Amazon EC2 instance, then select Networking flexible cost allocation under split cost allocation data in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console. Allocated line items appear in your CUR within 24 hours. FCA changes only how costs are shown in your reports. Your bill and total charges stay the same.

FCA is available at no additional charge. It's supported in all AWS commercial Regions except Middle East (Bahrain) and Middle East (UAE). It's also available in the China Regions. It is not available in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To learn more, visit the Networking FCA product page.

Developer Relations, Antigravity.

According to recent reports, I watched the discussion on agentic loops grow louder over the past few months. But for me, the reality is simpler: prompt engineering has shifted from individual tasks to systems design, and the harness around the model (not the model itself) is now my primary constraint in software engineering. In this article, I'll show you how to build and verify those harnesses so you can move from single-turn instructions to durable agentic loops in Google Antigravity.

You can categorize the work that we give to our agents into five distinct tiers, scaling from a quick question up through Agile tasks, stories, and epics to a continuous system:.

A simple question: This does not require an agent; an assistant can answer it.

A task / idea: This is one where a single prompt can zero-shot it. Use Google AI Studio to quickly transform ideas to functional prototypes.

In a recent development, an app / larger feature / story: The kind of work that required weekly planning and splitting into subtasks before AI. Use loops for execution and full-featured agents, like Google Antigravity. This tier is also where your steering moves upstream: You lock in the spec, the blueprint, and the executable tests before any loop runs.

In a recent development, A project / epic: A few features that make a cohesive story when connected. Loops here might help with planning too. This is also where one needs to go beyond simple turn-based prompting.

A system: An overview of all of the projects and tasks. This is where you write AGENTS.md project instructions, create skills, set up sidecars, wire up verification gates, and configure an instrument cluster to keep themselves on top of everything. Loops at this level make the biggest difference and come with similarly higher risks.

Figure 1: Five tiers of engineering work, from single prompts to verified agentic loops.

Recent findings suggest that the baseline of software development is shifting. This shift represents a basic law of human nature: we seek the highest leverage possible, moving from manual labor to delegation, and finally to orchestration. Because attention is the newly introduced bottleneck, anything that lets the work continue with less interruption could make a move in the right direction. By early 2026, empirical research of open-source projects estimated that coding agent adoption had reached between 22% and 29% of more than 128,000 active repositories on GitHub. Those who become proficient in agentic workflows now operate with a level of leverage that elevates their entire team's productivity. However, it also increases the cognitive load on everyone who is taking responsibility at the systemic level.

To understand this shift, let's trace the technical lineage of loops and set some high level expectations.

The academic seed was Yao et al.'s ReAct paper in October 2022, which interleaved reasoning traces with tool calls. ReAct beat reinforcement learning baselines by 34% on ALFWorld and 10% on WebShop by reasoning before acting, mirroring human nature: we perform better when verbalizing intends. Then came AutoGPT in early 2023, raising millions in venture funding. While early iterations of ReAct frequently spun in infinite loops, it proved developers wanted hands-off automation, highlighting the need for structural guardrails.

In a recent development, in mid-2025, developers ran stateless bash loops that piped prompts into command-line agents and reset context files on every tick. Resetting context prevents cognitive bloat and acknowledges that human memory limits also apply to models. Stateless bash loops worked only because the durable state lived outside the model: in Git history, in progress files, and in the test suite. It successfully built self-hosting compilers over months of automated runs. By spring 2026, major tool environments absorbed this pattern, shipping native commands like /goal to let agents run unattended loops.

Consider a theoretical example:.

Industry observers note that if you put your agent in a flat sequential chain to complete multiple tasks in a row, the agent's success rate degrades exponentially. When each of its individual steps operates as an independent probability event, a sequence of N steps has a cumulative success rate of pN. For instance, if you run a task requiring 20 consecutive file modifications with a model that has p = 0.95 accuracy, then you face a success rate of only 36%. Without your structural interventions, they will fail almost certainly.

It has been revealed that is 0.95 a real number? Treat it as an illustrative per-step reliability, not as a benchmark result. Even a frontier model reaches reliable multi-step outcomes only when it runs inside a verified harness. If your own per-step reliability sits closer to 75%, then the raw chain is already under 6% by step 10. The verification around the model sets the ceiling, which is why the loop matters.

This is why you need evaluation loops. A verification gate should not force your agent to retry indefinitely (which causes infinite spinning runaways). Instead, it should pinpoint where the error occurred and allow the model exactly one targeted retry to fix it. If your agent has a 95% base accuracy, and your evaluation loop has a 95% chance of spotting and fixing the error on that single retry, the effective step success probability rises to 0.95 + (0.05 x 0.95) = 99.75%.

That arithmetic assumes the check is independent of the worker, so the gate has to be an outside check. Compilers, test suites, and linters give you that for free, and behavioral evaluations let you assert on discrete tool calls and intermediate actions in seconds instead of waiting on a full end-to-end benchmark. For semantic judgments that a deterministic test cannot make, I pair models from different families so the reviewer does not share the worker's blind spot.

Even if fixing fails, just spotting the error with a 95% accuracy, lets you jump in and manually realign the system while keeping the same 99.75% subagent accuracy and only paying the cost of human-in-the-loop intervention.

The table below reveals the probability of completion across different chain lengths, comparing raw models to this single-retry course-correction topology:.

If each step in a chain adds approximately 1% of context in tokens, you end up with a chain that is not much longer than 50 steps before we require compression. A 95% base accuracy that can be evaluated (and course corrected with 95% accuracy for each dimension that we care about) should keep you at good success rates for such individual running agents. If you establish a scalable way to divide and conquer problems, you can apply similar principles to drive your subagents. As we can see, at 20 steps, a 95% accuracy paired with a single-retry corrective loop yields a 95% end-to-end success rate (assuming the correction itself stays under our 20 steps soft limit) while keeping context size reasonable. Note that there is no explicit requirement for the correction to be AI or human driven, but rather it needs to produce accurate and verifiable results.

According to recent reports, this is where you divide problems into tasks that require a small number of steps each. If a problem is more complex, it remains approachable, but it must be divided into smaller subproblems, and so on. For our example, this means allocating up to 20 steps for each level agent, task, and trajectory and another 20 steps for the next level supervisory agent to consolidate contributions. To prevent drift, establish separate evaluations at all subagent and supervisory levels with a final acceptance criteria.

Lastly, you must evaluate these metrics at least once for each level to verify that they measure the right target before running automation at a higher level. These are general estimations, but help you rapidly decide whether you should split a problem, repeat a step, or commit results and move on.

In practice, your numbers will look different, but the scaling laws will be similar.

Recent findings suggest that what started as a source of friction has now become one of my primary driving curiosities: how do we build automation when we still have a lot to learn about the craft itself? I have a few ideas.

To build a loop that does not run off a cliff, you must establish core guardrails that will keep accuracy high and will allow us to debug and intervene whenever necessary. Specifically, these are the pillars I identified:.

Durable state: Git-backed checkpoints ensure that your agent can resume work after a crash.

In a recent development, verification gates: Automated test suites and compilers deterministically check that the changes are correct. Write the acceptance criteria and the tests upstream, before implementation starts, and make one rule explicit in your project instructions: an agent cannot pass a gate by deleting or weakening a test. When done properly, gates can have >95% accuracy. However, you should be on the lookout for edge cases you might have forgotten about. Especially if verification, evaluation, or manual validation success rates diverge for any of your features.

Sources indicate that evals: Anything that cannot be deterministically verified but is key should have an evaluation or benchmark which you can later inspect for accuracy. Try to write them in a way that will keep answers to a simple yes or no and accuracy high, ideally over 95%. If you're getting results that point to confusion or unexpected failures, you probably need to split the criteria into simpler ones.

Halt conditions: Turn limits (as we saw above, 20 seems to be the sweet spot) and token or dollar cost ceilings stop runs before API budgets get out of control.

Standardized skills and instructions: Reusable utilities, documented in the SKILL.md format, preferably bundled with code and source of truth references. Pair them with an AGENTS.md that holds the project invariants every run load. Skills stay on disk until their description matches the task, so they do not eat into the 20-step context window.

Sources indicate that these pillars don't name a model version, but rather a model family. Individual model leads last only weeks. The asset that survives each release is the harness and its processes: the AGENTS.md instructions every run loads, the SKILL.md modules loaded only when relevant, the isolated Cloud Run sandbox where the loop runs around the clock, the deterministic checks, and the cross-model review. When a run fails or you have to intervene, patch your harness along with the code: a latest test, a line in AGENTS.md, a note in the skill. The next run inherits the lesson even though its context starts from zero.

Platforms like Google Antigravity have codified these patterns (/grill-me and /goal) into built-in primitives, shifting the work from custom scripts to platform capabilities for most straightforward use cases. The same harness files travel with the repository whether you run Google Antigravity 2.0, the agy CLI, or Antigravity inside VS Code, JetBrains, or Cursor. I would encourage you to give these a try. Do remember, however, to keep an eye on trajectory lengths and look for model confusion.

I myself frequently rely on the /goal primitives in Google Antigravity 2.0 when coordinating multi-turn tasks that require extensive validation and measurements before completion. To anchor this execution, use the /grill-me command for an interactive interview to lock in design constraints, invariants, and the tests that decide success before running /goal loops.

Constructing the metrics for this technical article and then editing it is just one example of how I use these execution loops.

By pairing /goal with /grill-me, you can establish an effective pair-programming dynamic: alignment on intent, followed by autonomy in execution.

To understand the evolution of loops, compare two distinct architectures for DIY agentic loops:.

According to recent reports, geoffrey Huntley's "Ralph" loop is a prime example of stateless architecture. Here's the simplest working version of an Antigravity CLI loop:.

While simple, the stateless loop is fragile for multi-file coordination because resetting context discards thinking logs.

A good agent skill could fix much of this limitation by instructing the model to output relevant progress reports in wiki-like markdown files and track changes by looking at git logs.

Still, this complexity has led to developer challenges in larger multi-agent environments, for which custom loops seem to hold the promise.

If you want to write a custom loop from scratch, here is a practical Python implementation using the Google Antigravity SDK. Specifically, this loop does the following actions:.

Initializes a supervisor session.

Verifies the output with the real test suite.

Feeds the actual failure output back for exactly one targeted retry.

Enforces strict call and token budgets.

According to recent reports, not every task inside it is equal, so neither is the model. The supervisor and the implementer run on Gemini 4 Carbon because orchestration, architecture, and the complex fixes need frontier reasoning, codebase search goes to Gemini 4 Hydrogen, and verification goes to a deterministic script that costs no tokens at all. The Guide to AI Tokenomics covers the budgeting side of this split. Far from being a production-ready solution, this is an experimental starting point that you can adapt to suit your individual needs:.

Figure 2: Budgeted supervisory verification loop in the Google Antigravity SDK.

The preceding implementation defines the following budgets:.

max_model_calls=20, a soft limit, counted across the supervisor's whole session.

max_total_tokens=200_000 as the cost ceiling.

Recent findings suggest that the SDK stops the turn and reports a stop_reason when either one trips. max_retries=1 limits each section: the first attempt plus one fix. If the verification still fails after that, the loop returns False and a human takes the seat instead of the model spinning until the budget runs out.

If you prefer not to build and host your own custom SDK loops from scratch, use Antigravity Agent, an autonomous, asynchronous coding agent. Antigravity Agent operates in a secure, isolated Google Cloud sandbox. This way you can create similar agentic loops by using managed agents to orchestrate execution plans under Google managed infrastructure. Alternatively, you can run the preceding loop inside a long-lived Cloud Run sandbox so that the loop keeps working after you close your laptop.

Industry observers note that you must establish a clear boundary for each of your validation systems that lets you  stay in control. No matter how perfect your loop, if you, as the responsible human, cannot sign off on your agent's output, there is minimal value in any of the artifacts it is producing. The good news is that building a quality evaluation scorecard or a loop algorithm uses a similar process to producing any other type of software artifact. So, much of the execution will be automated.

Finally, to make a sound judgment, you should observe each loop from the inside. As you see things working out, with this acquired confidence you step one level up. This is the only way to learn where the agent struggles and how to improve the process itself.

Not All Evidence Is Admissible: Evidence Governance for Tool-Augmented Medical Agents

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (260 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.22169v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Tool-augmented medical agents treat whatever their tools return as evidence. We show that this default is costly: medical tools fail silently, and a frozen reasoner cannot ignore what enters its context, so many cases it would have answered correctly are flipped to wrong once tool outputs are added. We call this evidence hijacking. $\mathcal{V}$-information explains the phenomenon: the reasoner has lost the option to ignore, so a tool output can carry negative usable information, and moving the decision of what to keep outside the reasoner restores that option. The theory further shows that part of any filtering gain comes merely from letting the reasoner see less, and only selection by content lets it see better. Building on this, we recast tool-augmented reasoning as evidence governance, which separates deciding what counts as evidence from the reasoner that answers, and propose context-independent evidence governance (CIEG), the first medical agent framework that rules, after acquisition, on whether each individual tool output may enter as evidence. Every tool output is written as a card that can be checked against the raw input; an independent checker that sees only the input and the cards decides which cards become evidence; and the reasoner answers from the admitted cards alone, with no training anywhere. On medical question answering, fundus glaucoma screening, and chest X-ray pneumonia classification, it achieves the highest accuracy among models of comparable scale, and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art tool-using agents and multi-agent systems built on the same backbone at lower cost.

Industry News: Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3045 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta.
  • Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.
  • Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

Recent findings suggest that meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that prepares, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

It has been revealed that muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the latest modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

Industry observers note that the language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

Industry observers note that only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

According to recent reports, muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

According to recent reports, the context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

Industry observers note that the Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

Sources indicate that use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

The Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

Sources indicate that video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:.

According to recent reports, as a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

The Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:.

In a recent development, the processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

According to recent reports, muse Spark Open can do text-only and multimodal tool calling. You can make the model call tools as follows.

Muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). Note that you don’t have to know about the internals, but it’s useful to check the channels the model routes to, in case you get low quality outputs. In the input message below:.

self is for reasoning, commentary are comments before and between tool calls visible to the end user, user is the final response.Tool-call routing is parsed as follows (assuming you have passed tools to apply_chat_template:.

Muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit, ready to use right away.

We tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens.

Recent findings suggest that once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning indicates up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer.

Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks.

The language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this:.

You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead.

Sources indicate that you can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section shows how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

In a recent development, first, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:.

In the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

Sources indicate that now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

In a recent development, the core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:.

Industry observers note that we trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

Muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

We combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

Recent findings suggest that we initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

It has been revealed that we tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

Muse Spark NVFP4 Browser Agent with OpenEnv and HF Sandboxes.

Hugging Face Sandboxes are sandboxes built on Hugging Face Jobs for easy code execution. The demo consists of three components:.

where the remote sandbox contains the environment and the browser as illustrated below.

You can easily try this with a few steps, described in the example. Start Inference Endpoint with Muse Spark Open (NVFP4 works well too!), add your endpoint URL as environmental variable, publish your OpenEnv server in Spaces and also provide that, then you can run the agent loop. Muse Spark Open sees the previous actions, system prompt, url and the screenshot of the browser to take an action, and nothing else (no DOM, no HTML code, nothing) so it’s a truly multimodal browser demo.

Finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.

Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.

Industry observers note that muse Spark Open is a full-size open-weight model from the Muse series. Start with the BF16 or NVFP4 checkpoint, or try one of the great llama.cpp quants. If you build something with Muse Spark Open, share it, and tell us in the repository’s discussions.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Long-Context Generation Is a Sampling Problem (When You Turn Up the Heat)

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (272 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.22148v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open-weight language models are widely observed to get worse the longer they generate. Often, attempts to fix this involve more training. At high temperature, The sampler, i.e. the rule that picks the next token out of the model's probabilities, decides whether long and agentic generation survives and/or thrives. We test 29 open-weight models from 1B to 122B parameters on ten established benchmarks plus needle retrieval out to one million tokens, covering SWE-bench Verified coding agents, long chain-of-thought reasoning, long-form writing, long structured output and long-context reading. Samplers that keep their pool of candidate tokens small and steady as temperature rises don't lose accuracy. Samplers that let in low-probability tokens fall apart. At temperature 2, coding agents running top-p, top-k or Top-H resolve 0 of 100 GitHub issues, while the same agents running top-nsigma resolve 46 to 62 and win every issue the two samplers disagree on, on three Qwen3.5 models. Over all benchmarks top-nsigma keeps a median 100% of its temperature-1 score where top-p keeps 26%. Counting how many tokens each sampler lets through explains why. In one Llama-3.1-8B story, going from temperature 1 to 2 grows top-p's pool from 4 tokens to 51,845 while top-nsigma stays at 3. Across 133 combinations of sampler setting and temperature, the typical pool size predicts judged quality (Spearman correlation of -0.77), and when we pick the pool at temperature 1 and only apply temperature afterwards, Top-H, min-p and p-less stop collapsing. At the default temperature of 1 most samplers perform about the same, We release all code and data to the public.

Substantial Brains, Tiny Board: Pupavision, an Agentic Physical AI Instrument for Monitoring Drosophila Pupariation and Lifecycle Transitions

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (293 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.22136v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Many biology experiments are limited by the availability and ease of use of instruments that monitor and record them. For example, the timing of pupariation in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, a widely used model organism, can provide biologically relevant information about growth regulation and is often recorded manually. Here, we present Pupavision, a small physical AI instrument built from a single-board Linux computer and a day/night camera for roughly 45 to 75 US dollars in parts. The key idea is that a frontier coding agent runs its agentic harness directly on the tiny board. The model thinks in the cloud, but the agent works on the device. The agent assists image capture, writes code to repair errors, and checks the experiment every day to keep raw data capture reliable. If recording stops, the researcher gets a ping on their mobile phone. A simple deterministic capture service records one image every ten minutes and never depends on the agent. We report a 26-day pilot in a fly incubator (about 3,580 frames), including eleven days in which the agent was logged out and capture continued, and a 51-hour outage whose cause led to the layered design. A researcher-in-the-loop workflow then produces per-vial pupariation curves by tracing selected pupae backward in time from a late reference frame. Future work will validate the assay for lifecycle tracking accuracy against expert-labeled data and expand real-time computer vision analysis. Pupavision offers a blueprint for do-it-yourself agentic instruments that put frontier intelligence on a tiny board, with deterministic code underneath. We present this as an early case study from a pilot lab deployment and contribute lessons learned toward a future where scientific domain experts are empowered by DIY agentic hardware.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

Industry observers note that apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline.

We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:.

Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All new data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

Alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

Sources indicate that the multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

Recent findings suggest that while still trailing frontier open-weight models, the newly introduced release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

We also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 highlights strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

According to recent reports, apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

It has been revealed that the results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

Recent findings suggest that all recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

The report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

In a recent development, access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been announced by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Recent findings suggest that thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team declared the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

In summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

If you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

Recent findings suggest that AWS Backup logically air-gapped vault now supports Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) DB instances. Logically air-gapped vaults are a type of AWS Backup vault that stores immutable, isolated backups, which are locked by default with AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode. Secure sharing across accounts and AWS Organizations enables direct restore, reducing recovery time from a data loss event.

According to recent reports, you can now protect your Amazon RDS DB instances in logically air-gapped vaults. A logically air-gapped vault stores immutable backups that are locked by default, and isolated with encryption using AWS owned keys or customer-managed keys. This helps reduce the risk of downtime, ensure business continuity, and meet compliance requirements.

Industry observers note that to get started, use the AWS Backup console, AWS Command Line Interface (CLI), or AWS SDKs. Assign your RDS DB instances to a backup proposal and specify a logically air-gapped vault in the same AWS Region as the copy destination. Share the vault for recovery or restore testing with other accounts using AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM), or safeguard vault access during account compromise using Multi-party approval. Once shared, you can initiate direct restore jobs from that account.

This support is available in most AWS Regions where both logically air-gapped vault and Amazon RDS are available. For more information and detailed regional availability, visit the AWS Backup documentation. To learn more about logically air-gapped vaults for RDS, read the launch blog and visit the feature documentation and pricing page.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.22131v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Whole image embeddings can under represent small objects and local attributes that distinguish relevant images for localized queries. We present LoCaR, a training free framework for localized text to image retrieval with frozen vision language models. LoCaR constructs and utilizes independent proposals (SAM2) focusing on the object so as to get a more localized representation that independently encodes each region using the frozen visual encoder. We further study paired-support adaptation as an optional residual that uses matched text region exemplars without updating the underlying encoders. We also introduce LOCFG, a Visual Genome derived benchmark designed to evaluate localized retrieval for smaller and more challenging referents. Across several vision language backbones, our results show that improving the region representation itself is the main source of gain.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The best things are never easy, and that mantra has stayed with Luke Magnan and Michael Jones as they have built Combined Ratio Solutions in the InsurTech landscape.
  • The solution was originally created after the duo built a policy administration tool for a client.
