💡 Key Takeaways
  • The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration.
  • Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs.
  • Industry observers note that residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, New Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration.

Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. The water can be released through turbines, generating electricity on demand. But an extreme, prolonged drought in the Colorado River Basin has resulted in dangerously low water levels in the Southwest’s two largest reservoirs, affecting the availability of this power source.

Industry observers note that residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, New Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases. Snowfall in the Rocky Mountains provides about 85% of the annual flow of the Colorado River. And in recent years, the river has seen record-low flows.

Recent findings suggest that two reservoirs along the Colorado River, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, have struggled to stay above the minimum level required for hydropower plants. At the end of September, Lake Powell’s depth was 3,518 feet, less than 1% above the level required to run the water through turbines that produce electricity at the Glen Canyon power plant. The Hoover Dam power plant requires 950 feet in Lake Mead, and that reservoir was 9% above the minimum in September.

Together, the two plants produced nearly seven terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, enough to serve over 2 million people.

According to recent reports, low water levels have been an ongoing struggle for the region, which has been in a drought for 27 years. Meanwhile, climate change is continuing to shift rainfall and snowfall patterns across the region and around the world.

The effects of climate change on hydropower aren’t entirely straightforward globally—some regions will see more rain and snow because of shifting weather patterns, while others are likely to see less.

But it’s playing a role for hydropower availability, according to one 2022 review study. Rising temperatures bring more droughts, warmer winters means less snow and ice to fill the reservoirs, and more variability in precipitation can lead to alternating floods and droughts, making the power source less reliable.

Hydropower production is likely to be at its lowest level in over a decade in 2026 and tick even lower in 2027, according to projections from the EIA.

According to recent reports, el Niño could provide some temporary relief. Sometimes this weather pattern can mean cooler, wetter conditions for the southern US. Heavy rains brought floods to the region in October and early November, and the water levels in Lake Powell rose more than 20 feet from their mid-September low. But the water is still quite low, and it’ll take much more to help reservoirs recover from decades of drought conditions.

Even as a changing climate complicates the availability of hydropower, the decline in capacity could push greenhouse-gas emissions higher. In 2023, energy-related greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 1.1% globally. A worldwide shortfall in hydropower generation accounted for about 40% of that rise, according to a report from the International Energy Agency.

Breaking: XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1189 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help consumers who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail.
  • A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y.
  • Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help consumers who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

Industry observers note that the models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer customers away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

Recent findings suggest that people use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.

We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

Industry observers note that for the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

It has been revealed that A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:.

In a recent development, in XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

According to recent reports, researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to people’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what consumers need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench at the moment covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.22119v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: Optimized Certainty Equivalents (OCEs) are an important class of risk measures for optimization and risk management that includes the Mean--Variance criterion, Expected Shortfall, the Entropic Risk Measure, and expectation. Despite their importance, economic axioms have not characterized OCEs. We propose a new axiom called Fair-Coin Compensation, which characterizes OCEs together with Strong Risk Aversion and Normalization. We interpret Fair-Coin Compensation through the fair assignment of two losses by a coin toss: transfers between two participants can remove the additional risk created by the random assignment. Adding further axioms yields sharper characterizations. Monotonicity yields standard OCEs; Positive Homogeneity, together with Prudence, yields Expected Shortfall; and Fair-Coin Independence yields the Entropic Risk Measure. We also axiomatize the Mean--Variance criterion using our novel axiom of Equal-Mean Randomization, which states that random assignment of two losses with the same expected value does not produce a risk measure above the average of their risk measures.

  • Recent findings suggest that starting today, access denied error messages for supported services and APIs will include a unique identifier that you can use to retrieve details of the authorization performed by the service.
  • To learn more about Access Troubleshooter and how it can help you resolve access denied errors efficiently, see the User Guide on troubleshooting access denied error messages.

AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) introduces Access Troubleshooter, a latest capability that gives you visibility into the full authorization context behind access denied errors so you can resolve them without trial-and-error. Previously, developers relied on the Amazon Resource Name (ARN) of the denying policy to debug a denial, with no visibility into the authorization context or other policies evaluated in the request that could contribute to the denial. This made troubleshooting access problems time-consuming and inefficient.

Recent findings suggest that starting today, access denied error messages for supported services and APIs will include a unique identifier that you can use to retrieve details of the authorization performed by the service. You gain visibility into what policies were evaluated for each request, the authorization context of those requests, and the results of the evaluation. This enables you to identify the root cause of authorization issues rapidly, streamlining your access management workflows and reducing time spent debugging permission problems.

To learn more about Access Troubleshooter and how it can help you resolve access denied errors efficiently, see the User Guide on troubleshooting access denied error messages.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AWS now supports credit splitting and transfers, enabling customers to divide any AWS credit into multiple smaller credits and transfer them to other linked accounts within their payer account.
  • It has been revealed that credit splitting and transfers eliminate hours of monthly manual chargeback work for FinOps teams and provide predictable credit budgets per team or business unit.
  • Credit splitting and transfers compose naturally with existing credit features, including credit-level sharing and credit pausing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AWS now supports credit splitting and transfers, enabling customers to divide any AWS credit into multiple smaller credits and transfer them to other linked accounts within their payer account. Previously, AWS applied credits starting with the owning account, then shared any excess with other accounts based on their usage, making it difficult for customers with large credits to direct precise amounts to specific teams or business units. FinOps teams can now split credits by dollar amounts, percentages, or even splits, and transfer each portion to the team that earned it.

It has been revealed that credit splitting and transfers eliminate hours of monthly manual chargeback work for FinOps teams and provide predictable credit budgets per team or business unit. Each split credit inherits the same expiration date and service eligibility as the original, and split credits retain sharing settings by default so unused balances flow to other eligible accounts. Accounts receive first-priority consumption for transferred credits.

Credit splitting and transfers compose naturally with existing credit features, including credit-level sharing and credit pausing. After a split, customers have full control over each resulting credit. For example, customers can split and share one credit across all intended accounts so multiple teams benefit, while restricting another split credit to a single account. They can also pause a credit earmarked for a future project, then resume it when needed.

You can split any credit type via the AWS Billing Console, CLI, or API. Partially consumed credits can be split, with the split applying to remaining balance only. Each credit family supports up to 100 splits, with a $100 minimum per split credit. Splits are permanent with no undo operation.

Credit splitting and transfers are available in all AWS commercial regions at no additional cost.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

According to recent reports, today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:.

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent.

In a recent development, the same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise looks include monthly credits for compute and inference.

On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

Recent findings suggest that the best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million consumers, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

Sources indicate that when a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the latest routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

Recent findings suggest that before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:.

Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO customers get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

Industry observers note that on model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:.

Sources indicate that in your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.21672v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Views are among the most valued and least measured attributes of a home. We present an open-data method that estimates the sea-view potential of every free fa\c{c}ade of every residential building at three floors (ground, middle and top; other floors take the nearest of them), from cadastral footprints with floor counts and a national terrain model. Run for 158,060 buildings of 21 municipalities on Spain's Costa del Sol in under an hour on two cores, it finds that 52 % of buildings see some sea from their top floor and 36 % have an open view (20{\deg} or more). Traced over a LiDAR surface in a pilot, scores agree with the model's inside cadastral footprints (96.7 % of viewpoints in the same class at 20{\deg}), but structures the cadastre does not record lower the sea seen from the top floor by 6.1--9.0{\deg} on average. Against the photographs of 93 homes for sale, labelled blind by AI models of two developers with ties decided by the author, the score has an AUC of 0.80 (95 % CI 0.70--0.89; 0.81 against the first-round labels); at 20{\deg} it is sensitive (0.90) but not specific (0.45). Dwelling figures depend on how dwellings are allocated to fa\c{c}ades and floors: 42 % of dwellings are on a floor with open-view potential under the main rule, and 12--45 % across the allocation, geometry and vegetation scenarios tested. As an application, higher-income census sections tend to have more modelled view potential within municipalities, with uncertain size and fragile inference (about two effective clusters); on terrain alone the difference largely disappears. Code and fa\c{c}ade-level data reproduce the main results.

It has been revealed that the fresh keyExchange value in the tlsDetails field of CloudTrail management and data events highlights the key exchange negotiated on each TLS connection, such as the hybrid post-quantum algorithm X25519MLKEM768 or a traditional algorithm such as x25519. For example, you can query your CloudTrail logs to find the user agents of S3 requests that did not use ML-KEM, then prioritize those clients for your post-quantum migration. The keyExchange value is recorded for requests to general purpose buckets, directory buckets, table buckets, and vector buckets, including requests made through AWS PrivateLink.

According to recent reports, key exchange details for S3 requests are available in all AWS Regions at no additional cost. Standard AWS CloudTrail pricing applies for S3 data events. To learn more, visit post-quantum TLS in the Amazon S3 User Guide and the CloudTrail record contents reference.

  • Sources indicate that the JWT authorizer works on Regional, edge-optimized, and private REST APIs, and is available in all commercial AWS Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.

Amazon API Gateway now offers a native JWT authorizer for REST APIs, a fresh authorizer type that validates JSON Web Tokens directly in the gateway. Until now, validating tokens from an OpenID Connect or OAuth 2.0 identity provider other than Amazon Cognito required a Lambda authorizer. You now configure token validation instead of writing and operating code for it.

In a recent development, you can define one or more issuers, the audiences accepted for each, the signing algorithms you permit, and any additional claims a token may present. API Gateway verifies each token's signature, issuer, audience, expiry, and claims on every request. You can attach one authorizer to many methods and require different scopes on each. This fits machine-to-machine APIs, mobile and web backends, and multi-tenant APIs that accept tokens from several identity providers.

Sources indicate that the JWT authorizer works on Regional, edge-optimized, and private REST APIs, and is available in all commercial AWS Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To get started, see Amazon API Gateway documentation and AWS blog post.

  • In a recent development, now, when you turn on Multipath Resilience for a cross-Region VPC peering connection, cross-Region Transit Gateway peering attachment, or cross-Region traffic on Cloud WAN, the network sends copies of each packet across physically diverse paths.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that AWS now offers a 99.999% availability service level agreement (SLA) for cross-Region traffic over Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) cross-Region peering, AWS Transit Gateway, and AWS Cloud WAN, with a new capability called Multipath Resilience. Multipath Resilience makes it easier to improve the resilience of mission-critical applications that send traffic across Regions, such as payment processing, financial trading, telephony, and live media streaming.

According to recent reports, the AWS backbone is highly resilient and connects Regions over physically diverse fiber paths. When a path fails, such as during a fiber cut, the network's automatic sub-second rerouting moves traffic to a healthy path. In the rare event that such mechanisms do not resolve the issue in a timely manner, such as when there's a partial degradation, it might take minutes for connectivity to be reestablished. Some applications, such as payment processing, financial trading, telephony, and live media streaming, can't tolerate single-digit seconds interruptions, let alone minutes of unavailability. Until now, customers running these applications relied on workarounds, including modifying their applications and operating systems to split a single connection into multiple connections, or replicating data into every Region to avoid cross-Region calls. These workarounds add complexity and don't always work, because applications can't control which network paths their traffic takes.

In a recent development, now, when you turn on Multipath Resilience for a cross-Region VPC peering connection, cross-Region Transit Gateway peering attachment, or cross-Region traffic on Cloud WAN, the network sends copies of each packet across physically diverse paths. It delivers whichever copy reaches your resources in the destination Region first and discards the duplicates. If one path drops packets, a copy is already in flight on another path, so your applications stay connected without waiting for the network protocols to reroute. Multipath Resilience moves this work out of your applications and into the network. Your applications keep using a single connection, with no changes to application code or operating systems, and no need to duplicate data to keep calls within a single Region.

Multipath Resilience is now generally available in US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (N. California), US West (Oregon), and Europe (Ireland).

To learn more, visit the Multipath Resilience documentation. For SLA details, visit the Multipath Resilience SLA. For pricing, visit the Amazon VPC pricing page.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when a WorkSpace is slow or won't connect, the IT administrator trying to help has traditionally had to dig through Amazon CloudWatch metrics, logs, and configuration data across multiple tools to find out why. And in the meantime, the user on the other end can't get their work done. In April this year, we released Amazon WorkSpaces Advisor, an AI-powered agent that helps IT administrators diagnose and fix WorkSpaces performance, connectivity and provisioning challenges and get users back to work faster. With Advisor, administrators can investigate a WorkSpace from the console and, in minutes, see the likely root cause and recommended actions they can take right away. Since then, we've continued to invest in Advisor so your team can spend less time chasing down issues one by one, and more time on the projects your business is counting on you to deliver.

Industry observers note that today, we're excited to announce the preview of proactive troubleshooting in WorkSpaces Advisor, which moves your team from reacting to individual tickets to staying ahead of challenges across your whole environment. Advisor can identify issues across your WorkSpaces, explain the likely cause of each one and recommend a fix. You don't need to start an investigation, wait for a user to report a problem, or set alarm thresholds first.

If the same problem affects many WorkSpaces, Advisor will show it as a single matter with the likely cause and a recommended fix. Your team fixes the root cause once instead of chasing the same symptom one WorkSpace at a time. For example, Advisor can tell you when a group of WorkSpaces became unhealthy at the same time, when WorkSpaces are running low on CPU or memory, or when a certificate your people need to sign in is about to expire. That gives you time to act before a small issue turns into an outage or a queue of support tickets. You'll find these issues in the WorkSpaces console.

Proactive troubleshooting also extends Advisor to your customers, which means fewer tickets reach your help desk and the ones that do come with better information. When a session is slow or won't connect, Advisor will tell users whether the problem is with their device, their network, or their WorkSpace. It then walks them through the fixes you've approved, such as restarting their WorkSpace. When an issue does need IT, the user gets a clear explanation to pass along, so your team starts from a diagnosis instead of "my WorkSpace is slow."  You stay in control because you decide which fixes users can make on their own, and you can turn this off for any directory.

Proactive troubleshooting is available in preview at no additional charge in AWS commercial Regions where Amazon WorkSpaces Personal is available. Troubleshooting for end consumers requires version 5.37 or later of the WorkSpaces client for Windows, with the latest experience turned on. Troubleshooting for users requires the WorkSpaces client for Windows version 5.37 or later with new experience. To get started, see the Amazon WorkSpaces Advisor Administration Guide.

According to recent reports, today, we are announcing that Amazon Elastic VMware Service (Amazon EVS) now supports the r7i.metal-24xl and r7i.metal-48xl Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) bare metal instance types for VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.x deployments. EC2 r7i instances are memory optimized, with custom 4th Generation Intel Xeon Scalable (Sapphire Rapids) processors, and designed to be used with external storage. With these instances possessing no local NVMe disks, Amazon EVS now supports VCF external principal storage with solutions such as Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP. With this launch, you can use the Amazon EVS Deployment Orchestrator (EDO) within the Solutions for EVS GitHub repository to fully automate the end-to-end deployment and configuration of your VCF 9.x environment on EVS.

With this release, you now have more options for running VMware-based Virtual Machines (VM) in your Amazon VPC - while keeping the same tools, skills, and operational processes, and full control of your architecture, configuration, and lifecycle of your environment.

Industry observers note that we are also launching a fresh Amazon EVS Agent Skill, which gives your AI Agents context to help you plan, deploy, and operate your Amazon EVS environments - from answering questions and recommending designs to generating blueprints and driving deployments with EDO. To get started, point the AI agent of your choice to the EVS Agent Skill file in the latest release of the EVS GitHub repository.

This release is available in all regions where Amazon EVS is offered. To learn more about Amazon EVS, visit the product detail page and the user guide.

  • Statement statistics measure every successful statement rather than sampling activity.
  • According to recent reports, statement statistics are available in all AWS Regions where Aurora DSQL is available.

Recent findings suggest that amazon Aurora DSQL now records statistics for each SQL statement your cluster runs and publishes them as Amazon CloudWatch OpenTelemetry (OTel) metrics. You can view them in Amazon CloudWatch Database Insights. For each statement, you see how often it runs, how long it takes, the rows it scans, returns, or changes, and the DPUs it uses.

Statement statistics measure every successful statement rather than sampling activity. Use them to find the statements that take the most time, run most often, or cost the most. In Database Insights, choose a statement under Top SQL to see its normalized SQL text and per-call charts. You can also query the metrics with PromQL in CloudWatch. Turn on statement statistics for each cluster in the Aurora DSQL console or the API when you create or revision the cluster.

According to recent reports, statement statistics are available in all AWS Regions where Aurora DSQL is available. Standard CloudWatch metrics and Logs charges apply, with no additional Aurora DSQL charge. To learn more, see monitoring SQL statements with statement statistics in the Aurora DSQL User Guide and CloudWatch pricing.

AWS Config reveals managed conformance packs

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (353 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AWS Config now offers managed conformance packs.
  • Previously, to evaluate resources against a framework such as PCI DSS or SOC 2, you started from a sample conformance pack template, customized it for your environment, and then updated it yourself whenever latest rules became available or the framework changed.
  • It has been revealed that managed conformance packs cover frameworks including PCI DSS v4, SOC 2, NIST SP 800-53 Rev.

AWS Config now offers managed conformance packs. AWS builds and maintains these packs for specific compliance and governance frameworks. When you deploy one, you choose a framework, and AWS Config evaluates your resources against it. AWS keeps the pack up to date as things change. When fresh AWS Config managed rules map to the framework's controls, or when the framework itself is revised, AWS updates your deployed pack automatically. Because AWS maintains a consistent pack definition in every supported Region, you can deploy the same framework across Regions without building or maintaining Region-specific rule sets. With managed conformance packs you no longer have to track framework changes or upgrade rules yourself.

Previously, to evaluate resources against a framework such as PCI DSS or SOC 2, you started from a sample conformance pack template, customized it for your environment, and then updated it yourself whenever latest rules became available or the framework changed. Managed conformance packs remove that work, so your coverage stays current without manual template changes. Each pack includes the managed rules available in the Region where you deploy it and adds new rules as they become available there, so you don't need a separate template for each Region. You can set rule parameters to fit your environment. Compliance results and compliance scores appear in the AWS Config console alongside your other rules and conformance packs.

It has been revealed that managed conformance packs cover frameworks including PCI DSS v4, SOC 2, NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, ISO/IEC 27001:2022, and CIS Controls, along with AI governance frameworks such as the EU AI Act and NIST AI RMF 1.0. For the full list, see the AWS Config documentation page.

Recent findings suggest that managed conformance packs are available in all AWS commercial Regions except Middle East (UAE) and Middle East (Bahrain). For the full list of supported Regions, see AWS Capabilities by Region. Evaluations are billed at standard conformance pack evaluation rates. To get started, open the AWS Config console and choose Conformance packs. To learn more, see the AWS Config Developer Guide and the AWS Config pricing page.
